stem: Grady’s description of the “new South” most directly expresses which of the following goals?

options.text: Restoring the plantation system with enslaved labor
options.misconception: Grady celebrates the old plantation economy and wants it back.

options.text: Replacing single-crop plantation agriculture with diversified industry
Returning the South to political independence from the Union
options.misconception: Grady wants the South to secede again.

options.text: Keeping the South free of Northern business and investment
options.misconception: Grady wants to shut Northern capital out of the South.

rationales.A: Grady says the South of slavery “is dead”; he praises its passing, not its return.
rationales.B: Grady contrasts the old South, which “rested everything on slavery and agriculture,” with a new South of “a hundred farms for every plantation” and “a diversified industry.” His goal is a mixed economy that moves beyond the single-crop plantation.
rationales.C: Grady says the South of secession “is dead” and celebrates “union and freedom.”
rationales.D: Background: Grady spoke to New York businessmen to win their investment; his program depended on Northern capital, not on shutting it out.
rationales.general:
1. Find the contrast. Grady sets the old South, built on slavery and one crop, against a new South of many farms and varied industry.
2. Read the goal in his own words. “A hundred farms for every plantation” and “a diversified industry” name what he wants built.
3. Test the other goals. He calls slavery and secession dead, so restoring them cannot be his aim.
4. Match the program. Background: Grady preached industrialization to Northern investors because the South needed their capital to build it.
Remember: a reformer’s program is the future he describes, not the past he buries.

stimulus.source_note: Henry W. Grady, “The New South,” address to the New England Society of New York, December 1886. Grady opens by quoting Benjamin H. Hill (1866). Portrait: Henry W. Grady, Library of Congress.
stimulus.text:
[Grady opens by quoting Benjamin H. Hill, 1866:]

“There was a South of slavery and secession — that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom — that South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour.”

“The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy, the oligarchs leading in the popular movement; a social system compact and closely knitted, less splendid on the surface, but stronger at the core; a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.”

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain speech with a Library of Congress portrait
